title: Trading system
author: Kamalghara_Z
selftext:
working on a real-time market scanner that processes 200+ stocks, multiple indicators, and live sentiment scoring — every second. 

\_The Stack

Node.js Cluster — spun across all CPU cores to parallelize per-stock computation instead of choking a single event loop

Redis — in-memory cache for LTP, OI, and volume snapshots so every read is O(1), not a DB round-trip

Redis Pub/Sub — decouples the calculation workers from the UI layer; workers publish, dashboards subscribe, zero polling

WebSockets — push updates straight to the frontend the moment a worker finishes a compute cycle 

\_What it's actually doing, per tick

Streaming live tick data across the full watchlist

Running momentum decay , volume delta, and OI shift calculations concurrently

Scoring bull/bear bias per stock and rolling it into an aggregate market sentiment (Neutral/Bullish/Bearish %)

Writing hot values to Redis, broadcasting deltas via Pub/Sub — no full-payload re-renders

The result A live "Trade Stats" panel showing regime (Trending/Chop/Trap), bull vs bear score, open interest skew, and per-stock signal grids — refreshing in near real-time without hammering the data source. 

The hard part wasn't the indicators — it was making 200+ parallel calculations, cache writes, and UI pushes feel instantaneous without race conditions or stale reads. Cluster + Redis + Pub/Sub turned out to be the right combination for this workload. 

Still iterating — next up is a data packet watch dog by AI Agent.

comments.author: Scott_Malkinsons
comments.body:
The setup makes me think you got something to sell, as most algo/ai traders aren't bothering with UI. That desk setup looks like a sales pitch, talking about "every second" sounds like a sales pitch. We both know in the real world of retail trading you don't need to be doing this every second, frankly you'd be better off with a buffered entry using limit or stop-limit orders to avoid slippage as you're, more likely than not, going in with market orders on the current setup.

there's a few things I see that either need clarification or improvement.

"Running momentum decay, volume delta, and OI shift calculations concurrently"

They aren't necessarily concurrent just because you're using Node cluster. Each worker is still generally executing JavaScript synchronously on its own process. You're parallelizing stocks/workloads across processes, not necessarily each indicator within a stock.

What you're actually doing is distributing momentum decay, volume delta, and OI shift calculations across worker processes.

Beyond that, "cache writes, and UI pushes feel instantaneous without race conditions or stale reads"

Redis + Pub/Sub doesn't automatically eliminate race conditions or stale reads. You still need to design around things like: ticks arriving out of order, duplicate ticks, worker A processing an older tick after worker B processed a newer one, Redis updates occurring in the wrong order, Pub/Sub messages being lost if a subscriber disconnects, multiple workers attempting to update the same stock

For your "no full-payload re-renders" claim. That's if you're actually sending deltas but you seem to be sending ticks. Deltas example: AAPL, price: 227.41, bullScore: 72, oiSkew: +14 rather than sending the entire 200-stock dataset every second.

Also if the system is genuinely processing live ticks (and I do have my doubts about this), you probably don't want every worker independently consuming the raw market feed. A cleaner architecture is something like: Market Data Feed > Ingestion Process > Redis / Stream> Worker Processes > Indicator + Signal Engine >  Redis> Pub/Sub.

And for 200 stocks, you can potentially simplify this substantially. You may not actually need Node Cluster yet. If the calculations aren't CPU-heavy, a single Node process with efficient data structures and asynchronous I/O could comfortably handle the workload. The architecture becomes much more compelling if you're doing things like rolling calculations over thousands of historical observations, multiple timeframes, sentiment/NLP processing, etc.
